newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Rustle of windfall tax spooks UK utilities.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Rustle of windfall tax spooks UK utilities.

text.p: Shares in many of Britain's privatised utilities dipped on Friday as the market recoiled at the threat that the incoming Labour government would impose a "windfall" tax on their profits.
"People have known about the risks for a long time but when they're in your face there's bound to be a bit of a kneejerk reaction," a market-maker said.
But analysts said the falls may have been overdone after the Labour Party's landslide election victory on Thursday.
Labour has long said it would impose a levy on formerly state-owned utilities if it came to power, saying that they had been laxly regulated and sold off too cheaply, allowing excess profits.
Leading the way, National Power Plc was off 18-1/2 pence at 515p by mid afternoon while PowerGen Plc was down 22.5p at 632p. The FTSE-100 index was up 13.2 points at 4,458.2.
"I don't know why those firms have been particularly affected. Nothing has changed fundamentally," Merrill Lynch utilities analyst Andrew Wright said. "This is a buying opportunity."
Among water stocks, Hyder Plc was off 31.5p at 820p with United Utilities Plc down 20p at 650p.

Labour's finance spokesman Gordon Brown, likely to be named chancellor of the exchequer (finance minister), has said the windfall tax would comfortably finance a three billion pound ($4.8 billion) plan to help the young and long-term unemployed back into work.
"The key moment will be when Brown stands up and starts saying things about the tax," said another analyst. This could be as early as his expected mini-budget within the next two months.
Investment bank UBS said in a recent report there were major uncertainties about the size of the tax, who will pay, its legality and the basis of allocation.
Many analysts believe the windfall tax, which will be a major plank of Brown's first budget, could raise up to five billion pounds, although figures as high as 10 billion pounds have been suggested.
A level of tax to yield five billion pounds appeared to have been factored into share prices, analysts said.

Labour refused to be drawn on specific targets for the tax. Its "excess profits" statements could mean the net being cast wide enough to include British Telecom, the former British Gas utility Centrica, Railtrack and airports operator BAA Plc, as well as the electricity and water companies.

Labour has reserved its fiercest criticism for the latter, condemning them for hefty dividends and fat executive pay packets, while it says more than 800 million gallons of water supplies leak out of pipes dailies as Britons face a hosepipe ban heading into the summer.

Brown said earlier this week that the British people would be outraged at the expected profits of the companies and would "regard a government that failed to deal with this problem as a government that had failed".
The privatised water and electricity companies report annual results in May and June.
